issues.issue: The execution date in the opening sentence is illegible and self-contradictory ("made on / Oo} 24) OO , 2000"), so the date the Trust was created is not fixed by the words used. Every other document dates the Declaration October 24, 2000, but this provision does not say so legibly.

Recital (c) says the Trustee "commits to limiting participation in the Trust to less than 100 Shareholders," while operative Section 4.4 says the Trust shall not have "more than 100 Shareholders" — the recital and the operative term set different ceilings. A court would have to decide whether the recital's commitment controls the operative section.

The definition cross-refers "Covered Person" to Article Nine, Section 9.2, but Section 9.2 is "Trustee Action; Expert Advice; No Bond or Surety" and contains no such definition; the term is actually defined in Article Eight, Section 8.1. The mis-citation leaves the defined class of protected persons to be fixed by construction.

"Majority Shareholder Vote" is defined, but Section 4.8 denies Shareholders any right to vote and Section 2.2(b) uses a two-thirds vote rather than a majority, so the defined term has no operative field. A court would have to decide whether the definition presupposes voting rights the instrument elsewhere withholds.

The definition fixes "Net Asset Value" at the Series level, while Sections 4.5, 5.2 and 5.4 all operate on "Net Asset Value per Share," a figure this definition does not supply. The per-Share measure a redeeming Shareholder is entitled to therefore rests on an undefined derivative of the defined term.

"Outstanding Shares" excludes redeemed Shares held in treasury, but Section 5.2 provides that upon redemption Shares "shall not be canceled" and may be reissued, leaving unclear whether redeemed Shares drop out of the count. That count drives the two-thirds removal threshold in Section 2.2(b) and the 100-Shareholder limit in Section 4.4.

"Shareholder" is limited to a "record owner of Outstanding Shares," yet Section 4.4 counts beneficial owners holding through flow-through entities as Shareholders for the 100-holder limit. The two treatments of who is a Shareholder cannot both be applied consistently.

"Shares" are defined as "transferable units of interest," which cannot be squared with Section 4.9, under which the beneficial interest "shall not be transferable and any purported transfer shall be void." A court would have to decide which characterization governs the alienability of a Shareholder's interest.

The definition is circular — "'Trust' means the Trust, created hereby" — and so supplies no content beyond the preamble. Whether "Trust" includes the separate Series must be worked out from Article Four instead.

The definition contemplates a plurality of Trustees "acting collectively," while Section 2.2(a) provides that "[t]here shall be one trustee." The plural apparatus of the definition has no application to the single corporate Trustee actually serving.

The conclusive-determination sentence ("[a]ny determination made by the Trustee in good faith as to what is in the interests of the Trust shall be conclusive") cannot be squared with Section 3.3, which subjects the Trustee to an ERISA prudent-person standard, and with Section 8.5, which preserves ERISA liability. Good faith alone would displace a duty the instrument elsewhere imposes.

"There shall be one trustee, except as the Trustee may determine otherwise" cannot be squared with Sections 2.3 and 2.4, which operate through "the remaining Trustee or Trustees" and "a majority of the Trustees." With a sole trustee those mechanisms have nothing to work on.

Removal of the Trustee "by a vote of at least two-thirds of the Outstanding Shares at a meeting of the Shareholders" is flatly contrary to Section 4.8, which says Shareholders have no right "to appoint, select, vote for or remove the Trustee." The same conflict attends the clause's reference to holding office "until its successor is elected."

Succession depends on "the remaining Trustee or Trustees" appointing a replacement, but under Section 2.2(a) there is only one trustee, so resignation or removal of that sole Trustee leaves no one empowered to fill the vacancy. The provision supplies no fallback mechanism.

The section vests "all the powers hereunder" in "the remaining Trustees" during a vacancy and allows delegation "to any other Trustee or Trustees," neither of which can operate under the single-trustee structure of Section 2.2(a). Who holds the powers when the sole Trustee's office is vacant is left unresolved.

The closing sentence is garbled and carries a broken cross-reference ("each Shareholder shall have as provided in Article Four, 1.2 proportionate undivided beneficial interest"), so the nature and measure of a Shareholder's interest cannot be read off the text. The stray "1.2" corresponds to no section of this Declaration.

Compensation "as may be fixed from time to time by the Trustee" itself sits against the last sentence of Section 6.1, which bars retention of the Trustee or its affiliates "for additional compensation beyond that disclosed and agreed to in the various written agreements entered into between Shareholders and the Trustee." Whether the Trustee can unilaterally set fees beyond the securities lending agreement's agreed split is left open.

Clause (h) makes the power to sell or exchange assets "subject to Article Eleven, Section 11.4," but this Declaration ends at Article Nine and contains no Section 11.4; clause (l) likewise trails off ("[t]o the full extent permitted by Section 12-") and points liabilities to "Article Four, Section 4.5," which concerns investments rather than Series liabilities. The limits on the enumerated powers thus cannot be located in the instrument.

The closing "[n]otwithstanding" paragraph requires the Trustee to comply with the affiliated-transaction prohibitions of 1940 Act Section 17(a), (d) and (e) and the leverage prohibitions of Section 18 as if registered, which cannot be squared with Section 3.2's permission to deal with affiliates and clause (o)'s power to borrow and pledge Trust assets. A court would have to decide which of the two governs an affiliated or leveraged transaction.

The permission to buy from, sell to and lend Trust assets to the Trustee, its officers, its investment adviser and transfer agent cannot be squared with the final paragraph of Section 3.1, which requires the Trustee to comply with the 1940 Act Section 17(a), (d) and (e) prohibitions on affiliated transactions as if the Trust were registered. The two provisions give opposite answers on self-dealing.

The ERISA prudent-person standard of care imposed here cannot be squared with Section 8.1, which exculpates the Trustee for everything short of bad faith, gross negligence, willful misconduct or reckless disregard, or with Section 8.4's replacement of duties existing at law or equity. Section 8.5 saves only Part 4 ERISA duties, so the standard's reach as to non-ERISA Shareholders is contested.

The passage on distributions and equal beneficial interest is garbled and its qualifier — "except to the extent affected by expense allocations" — has no stated limit, so how far a Share's proportionate interest may be diluted by allocated expenses is undetermined. The provision gives no benchmark for a permissible allocation.

Clause (iii) empowers the Trustee to establish Shares of any Series with "voting powers," which cannot be squared with Section 4.8's flat statement that Shareholders have no right to vote or otherwise participate in the business decisions of the Trust. Whether any Share may carry a vote is left to construction.

The Trustee "may, in its sole discretion, establish eligibility requirements," yet Recital (b) and Section 4.4 make qualified-purchaser status and the 100-Shareholder cap conditions the Trust must satisfy — a mandatory limit expressed as a discretion. Whether the Trustee is obliged, not merely permitted, to screen investors is unresolved.

This section caps the Trust at "not more than 100 Shareholders," while Recital (c) records a commitment to "less than 100 Shareholders"; the two ceilings differ by one and a court would have to decide whether the recital controls. The section's own text is also partly illegible on the point.

Shares are credited at the Net Asset Value "next determined after the investment Is received or accepted as may be determined by the Trustee," leaving two different triggering events — receipt or acceptance — and no rule for choosing between them. The pricing of a subscription therefore turns on an unresolved alternative.

Assets and general liabilities not "readily identifiable as belonging to any particular Series" are allocated as the Trustee "deem[s] fair and equitable," with the allocation declared "conclusive and binding," and the charging sentence is garbled. The standard governing cross-Series allocation of losses and expenses is thus both vague and self-judging.

The promise that a Series' debts are enforceable "against the assets of such Series only" sits against Article Seven, which gives the Trustee a lien on the assets of each Series for expenses allocable to more than one Series and for losses incurred in administering the Trust. A creditor-Trustee's cross-Series lien and the inter-Series shield cannot both be given full effect.

The register is made "conclusive as to the identity of Shareholders of record," yet Section 4.4 treats certain beneficial owners holding through flow-through entities as Shareholders who never appear on that register. Which record governs the Shareholder count is left unsettled.

The power to "make rules governing the transfer of Shares" presupposes transfers that Section 4.9 declares void and of no effect, and the Subscription Agreement in turn says transfers may be made with the Trustee's consent. Whether Shares are transferable at all cannot be answered from these provisions together.

The denial of any right to vote for or remove the Trustee or to amend the Declaration cannot be squared with Section 2.2(b), which allows removal of the Trustee by a two-thirds vote of Outstanding Shares, or with the proviso to Section 9.7 giving Shareholders the right to vote on amendments submitted to them. A court would have to decide which provision yields.

Absolute non-transferability here cannot be squared with the Subscription Agreement's statement that "transfers of Shares in the Trust may be made only with the consent of the Trustee in its sole discretion," nor with Section 4.7(b)'s power to make rules governing Share transfers. The instruments give inconsistent answers on whether a consented transfer is effective.

The section commands that "[e]very written obligation of the Trust or any Series shall contain" a limitation-of-recourse statement and in the same breath provides that omission of the statement has no consequence, so the obligation is directive with no sanction. It also measures Shareholder liability by the law of "a private corporation for profit organized under the General Corporation Law of the State of Maryland," a body of law it does not identify precisely.

Distributions are to be made "pro rata ... in proportion to the number of Shares," which cannot be squared with the First Amendment's Section 9.1 requiring Subchapter K capital accounts and allocation of income and loss by percentage interest and full netting methodology, nor with Section 4.1's carve-out for expense allocations. Which allocation rule governs a distribution is unresolved.

The redemption right is keyed to "the close of business on each Business Day," but "Business Day" is nowhere defined in Article One or elsewhere in this Declaration, even though the Confidential Memoranda expressly say "Business Day (as defined in the Declaration of Trust)." The frequency and timing of the redemption right therefore rest on an undefined term.

The suspension power — "a period not exceeding seven days" in the Trustee's judgment — cannot be squared with the Confidential Memorandum for the CI Term Trust, which conditions redemption on seven business days' notice and reserves a right to postpone payment or suspend redemptions "in certain circumstances as specified in the Declaration of Trust." The two documents describe different redemption and suspension mechanics.

Net Asset Value is to be determined "in a manner consistent with the 1940 Act," but the Trust is unregistered and the Act supplies several valuation regimes (market value versus Rule 2a-7 amortized cost), so the phrase fixes no method. The Confidential Memoranda instead say assets "will be valued each Business Day at their then current market value."

This section is expressly premised on the Trustee "postpon[ing] payment of the redemption price" "as referred to in Section 5.2," but Section 5.2 contains no postponement power — only a suspension of the right of redemption for not more than seven days. The trigger for suspension therefore points to something Section 5.2 does not say.

The bar on retaining the Trustee or its affiliates "for additional compensation beyond that disclosed and agreed to in the various written agreements entered into between Shareholders and the Trustee" cannot be squared with Section 2.6 and Section 3.1(k), which let the Trustee fix and pay itself compensation, or with the Confidential Memoranda, under which Wells Fargo appointed itself investment manager and may take fees it determines to be reasonable. Which regime limits the Trustee's fees is left open.

"[C]ontracts for such other services deemed necessary or appropriate by the Trustee" is an open-ended catch-all appended to the specific categories of transfer agency, accounting and administration, with no ejusdem generis limit stated. Its reach against the enumerated specifics would have to be construed.

This section allows "broker-dealers, brokers, banks or trust companies" to serve as custodian, whereas Section 3.1(d) confines custodians to banks, trust companies, members of a national securities exchange "or other entities permitted by the Commission to serve as such." The two lists of eligible custodians do not match.

Validating affiliate contracts so long as they are "reasonable and fair" cannot be squared with the closing paragraph of Section 3.1, which requires compliance with the 1940 Act Section 17(a), (d) and (e) prohibitions on affiliated transactions as if the Trust were registered. A self-dealing contract could satisfy one and violate the other.

The Article opens "Subject to Article Four, Section 4.4," but Section 4.4 is the publicly-traded-partnership/100-Shareholder provision and says nothing about expenses; the qualification points to a section that cannot qualify it. What limits the expense obligation is therefore indeterminate.

The exculpation, which imposes liability only for "bad faith, gross negligence, willful misconduct or reckless disregard," cannot be squared with the Securities Lending Agreement, under which "[t]he Bank assumes the risk of loss arising from negligent and fraudulent operation of its Securities Lending Program," or with the Confidential Memoranda, which preserve liability for simple "negligence." Whether ordinary negligence is actionable turns on which document governs.

The same limitation cannot be squared with Section 3.3, which binds the Trustee to the ERISA prudent-person standard, and with Section 8.5, which withholds Article Eight's protection for Part 4 ERISA duties. The scope of the exculpation as against a fiduciary duty imposed elsewhere in the instrument is contested.

Mandatory indemnification "to the fullest extent permitted under the Maryland Act" for "all liabilities and expenses" incurred by virtue of being a Covered Person carries no exclusion for bad faith, gross negligence or willful misconduct, unlike Section 8.1 and unlike the Confidential Memoranda's carve-outs. Whether a Covered Person held liable under Section 8.1 may nonetheless be indemnified is unresolved.

The closing proviso relieves the Trust of paying "the expenses of any agent acting pursuant to a written contract with the Trust, except to the extent required by such contract," which cuts against Section 8.2(a)'s mandatory indemnification of every Covered Person, a class that includes agents. Which of the two governs an agent's advancement claim is left open.

The subsection speaks of "[a]ny repeal or modification of this Article Seven," but it sits in Article Eight; Article Seven is the expenses article. The anti-retroactivity protection therefore names the wrong article on its face.

The trigger — personal liability "solely by reason of his or her being ... a Shareholder and not because of his or her acts or omissions or for some other reason" — is internally contradictory, since "or for some other reason" negates the "solely" it qualifies. When indemnity is owed cannot be read off the sentence.

The agreement that this Declaration's provisions "replace such other duties and liabilities" existing at law or in equity cannot be squared with Section 3.3's ERISA prudent-person duty, Section 8.5's ERISA carve-out, or the Securities Lending Agreement's assumption of the risk of negligent operation of the program. Whether common-law and contractual duties survive the Declaration is precisely what would be litigated.

The exception is confined to "any responsibility, obligation, or fiduciary duty imposed upon the Trustee by Part 4 of ERISA," and by naming only that source it invites the argument that all other duties — including the negligence standard in the Securities Lending Agreement — are extinguished by Article Eight. The expressio unius reading of the enumerated exception is the defect.

"This Declaration creates a trust and not a partnership" cannot be squared with the First Amendment, which deleted this section and substituted a Federal Tax Status provision classifying each Series as a partnership, nor with Recital (c), Section 4.4 and the Confidential Memoranda, which treat the Trust as a partnership for tax purposes. A court would have to decide the character of the arrangement and the effect of the deletion.

Reliance on counsel is made "subject to the provisions of Article Seven," but Article Seven concerns expenses of the Trust; the liability provisions are in Article Eight. The qualification on the Trustee's protection therefore cites the wrong article, and the clause also protects the Trustee both for following and "for failing to follow" the advice.

Clause (i) permits a sale of substantially all assets "to another Series" for consideration that "may include Shares of or interests in such Series, entity, or series thereof," the later language presupposing a transferee entity the clause never authorizes. The class of permitted transferees cannot be read off the text, and the perpetual-existence sentence is immediately undone by the dissolution power that follows.

Making the Trustee's own "best interests" determination "conclusive and binding" sits against Section 3.3's prudent-person standard and Section 8.5's preservation of ERISA duties, which contemplate review of the Trustee's judgment. Whether the dissolution decision is truly unreviewable is left to construction.

Discharge of "the Trustee and the Trust ... of any and all further liabilities and duties" on termination cannot be squared with Section 8.3's indemnity to former Shareholders and Section 8.2's indemnification of Covered Persons, which contemplate obligations surviving winding up. Whether termination extinguishes accrued claims is unresolved.

The second paragraph refers to a merger agreement "approved by the Trustees in accordance with this Section 4," but there is no Section 4 of Article Nine; the section is 9.4. The mis-citation leaves the approval requirement pointing at nothing.

The choice of "the Maryland Act and the applicable laws of the State of Maryland" cannot be squared with the Securities Lending Agreement, Section 12 of which chooses Minnesota law, or with Section 9(a) of the Subscription Agreement, which does the same for the same investment relationship. Which law governs a Shareholder's claim against the Trustee is a live question.

The closing proviso — "that Shareholders shall have the right to vote on any amendment submitted to them by the Trustee in its discretion" — cannot be squared with Section 4.8, under which Shareholders have no right to amend the Declaration or to participate in the business decisions of the Trust. The premise that the Declaration "does not confer any independent rights to Shareholders" also sits uneasily with the redemption right in Section 5.2.

This Fiscal Year section is numbered 9.7, the same number already used by the Amendments section immediately above it, so any reference to "Section 9.7" is ambiguous. The duplicate numbering is a mechanical defect on the face of the instrument.

The Trustee alone, "with the advice of counsel," may determine that a provision conflicts with the Maryland Act, the 1940 Act "or with other applicable laws and regulations," whereupon the provision is "deemed never to have constituted a part of this Declaration" — a retroactive excision governed by no stated standard and by no other party's participation. The open-ended reference to "other applicable laws and regulations" gives the power no boundary.

Inspection rights are denied "[e]xcept as expressly required under the Maryland Act or conferred under other applicable law," so the clause's actual effect depends entirely on external law it does not identify. Whether a Shareholder may inspect the Trust's books cannot be answered from the provision itself.

The operative allocation language is garbled and incomplete ("shall allocate (i) all income ... ors percentage Interest in the serie e d and loss based on the full netting methodology"), so how income, gain and loss are to be allocated among investors cannot be read off the text. It also uses "IRC," a term the Declaration never defines, having defined "Code" in Article One instead.

Classifying each Series as a separate partnership with Subchapter K capital accounts cannot be squared with Section 5.1, which requires distributions strictly pro rata by number of Shares, nor with Section 4.4's insistence that the Trust not be treated as a publicly traded partnership. The tax characterization and the distribution mechanics pull in different directions.

"All other terms and conditions of the Declaration are reaffirmed as written" reaffirms provisions that the new Section 9.1 contradicts — notably Section 5.1's pro rata distribution rule and the trust-not-partnership premises in Recital (c) and Section 4.4. The blanket reaffirmation supplies no priority rule for the resulting inconsistency.
